qs.q: Which cellular component contains the majority of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activity within the hepatocytes?
qs.e: About 80% of AST activity in the liver is located in the mitochondria, while only 20% is cytosolic. In contrast, other options do not accurately represent the primary hepatic compartmentalization of AST.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: AST is an intracellular enzyme that transfers amino groups between aspartate and α‑ketoglutarate. It is released into blood when hepatocytes, cardiac or skeletal muscle cells are damaged. Clinicians use its level and ratio to ALT to infer tissue injury and guide management.

sections.p: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) catalyzes the reversible transfer of an amino group from aspartate to α‑ketoglutarate, forming oxaloacetate and glutamate. It is present in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, brain and red blood cells.
b: Key reaction: Aspartate + α‑ketoglutarate ⇌ Oxaloacetate + Glutamate

sections.p: AST is a cytosolic enzyme that participates in amino‑acid metabolism and the urea cycle. When cells are injured, AST leaks into the bloodstream, raising serum concentration.

AST activity is regulated by substrate availability and cellular energy status. It is not tightly controlled by feedback loops, so serum levels mainly reflect cell integrity rather than enzyme synthesis.

AST is a routine part of liver function tests. Its level, trend, and ratio to ALT help differentiate liver disease etiology and severity.

t.b: High AST indicates cell injury; magnitude and trend guide urgency.

faq.q: Why is AST less specific than ALT?
faq.a: AST is found in many tissues; ALT is mainly hepatic, so ALT rises more selectively with liver injury.

faq.q: Can AST be normal in liver disease?
faq.a: Early or mild liver injury may show normal AST; serial testing or imaging may be needed.
Use ALT and other liver enzymes (ALP, GGT) to assess hepatic injury; consider clinical context and imaging.
